title: Digital Twin Control Framework Uncovers Individualized Cross-Scale Links Between Functional Connectivity Deviations, Communication Impairment, and Molecular Mechanisms in Autism.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is hallmarked by pronounced inter-individual heterogeneity in brain function and clinical manifestations. Conventional neuroimaging studies yield highly inconsistent findings, as extrinsic confounding factors and intrinsic disease heterogeneity mask ASD-specific functional connectivity (FC) signatures, hampering the identification of individualized neural mechanisms linked to symptom severity. METHODS: We developed a digital twin control analytical framework based on deep contrastive learning. By comparing each ASD participant with their matched digital twin control, we quantified individual-specific FC deviations. Principal component analysis was applied to extract the core aberrant pattern, followed by multi-dimensional analyses and validation including clinical correlation, transcriptomic decoding, neurotransmitter and mitochondrial co-localization, as well as disease and cognitive enrichment. RESULTS: The model effectively disentangled disease‑related from non‑disease‑related variations. The identified dominant aberrant FC pattern was significantly associated with Autism Diagnostic Observation Schedule (ADOS) communication scores, suggesting its associated with to communication impairment. This pattern showed convergent associations with synaptic pathways, excitatory/inhibitory neuronal signatures, critical developmental windows and subcortical structures, and exhibited negative spatial association with multiple neurotransmitter systems and mitochondrial respiratory complexes. Biological validation further supported its ASD specificity and communication‑related cognitive relevance. CONCLUSIONS: Leveraging the twin control analytical framework, this study provides an exploratory cross-scale framework linking individualized FC deviations with clinical, transcriptomic, neurochemical, and mitochondrial maps. The findings indicate that communication difficulties in ASD may partly arise from multi-scale disturbances in neural integration, social-perceptual processing and activity-dependent cellular energy regulation.

title: Clinical, immunological and metabolic features and gut-brain axis markers in children with autism spectrum disorder and TORCH-associated central nervous system involvement.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Autism spectrum disorders (ASD) have heterogeneous etiologies, with TORCH infections potentially contributing to neurodevelopmental disruption through central nervous system injury and gut-brain axis dysfunction. METHODS: A prospective comparative study enrolled 280 children aged 3-10 years with ASD: 112 with TORCH-associated central nervous system (CNS) involvement (main group) and 168 with idiopathic ASD (comparison group), alongside 25 healthy controls. Assessments included clinical/neurological features, autism severity, gastrointestinal symptoms, pro-inflammatory cytokines, metabolic markers, neuron-specific enolase (NSE), fecal zonulin, and brain MRI. TORCH pathogens were detected by PCR from saliva samples. RESULTS: TORCH-associated ASD exhibited a more severe phenotype with greater frequencies of delayed speech, cognitive impairment, sleep disturbance, hyperactivity, emotional-behavioral dysregulation, epileptiform manifestations, and gastrointestinal symptoms. Severe ASD was significantly more common in the TORCH group. Laboratory analyses revealed significantly elevated interleukin-1β, interleukin-8, tumor necrosis factor alpha, homocysteine, ammonia, uric acid, NSE, and fecal zonulin, with reduced folate. Fecal zonulin was positively correlated with inflammatory markers and neuron-specific enolase. MRI more frequently demonstrated periventricular gliosis, ventriculomegaly, subependymal abnormalities, and diffuse residual organic changes. CONCLUSIONS: In this cohort, ASD with clinical evidence of TORCH-associated CNS involvement was associated with greater clinical severity and higher serum inflammatory, metabolic, neuronal-injury, fecal-zonulin, and structural MRI measures than ASD without such evidence. The cross-sectional design and limitations of salivary PCR preclude causal attribution to TORCH infection.

title: Histone deacetylase 6 (HDAC6)-mediated α-tubulin (K40) deacetylation and microtubule destabilization disrupt autophagosome-lysosome fusion in PBDE-47-induced neurotoxicity.
abstract: 2,2',4,4'-tetrabromodiphenyl ether (PBDE-47) is a pervasive environmental brominated flame retardant that accumulates in nervous tissues and induces persistent neurotoxicity. Emerging evidence indicates that PBDE-47 perturbs neuronal autophagy, yet the definitive upstream molecular mechanism remains uncharacterized, hindering the development of effective protective strategies. This study was performed to clarify the toxic regulatory cascade and explore feasible pharmacological interventions using in vivo neonatal rat hippocampal tissue and in vitro PC12 neuronal cell models. Animals were neonatally exposed to PBDE-47 (0.1, 1.0, 10.0 mg/kg·bw), and PC12 cells were treated with PBDE-47 (1, 10, 20 µM) for mechanistic exploration. Results showed that PBDE-47 dose-dependently upregulated histone deacetylase 6 (HDAC6), decreased α-tubulin (K40) acetylation, and destabilized neuronal microtubules. Such microtubule structural damage impaired autophagosome retrograde trafficking, blocked autophagosome-lysosome fusion, and eventually caused neuronal loss, synaptic protein reduction, and cognitive impairment. For mechanism validation and rescue experiments, 1 mg/kg·bw paclitaxel (PTX) and 1 mg/kg·bw tubastatin A (TBA) were administered to neonatal rats, whereas 12.5 nmol/L PTX and 10 µmol/L TBA were used for PC12 cell treatment to stabilize microtubules and selectively inhibit HDAC6, respectively. Both pharmacological interventions effectively restored tubulin acetylation, rescued defective autophagic flux, and mitigated PBDE-47-induced neuronal injury, with TBA showing better applicability due to its high blood-brain barrier permeability and biosafety. Behavioral tests in vivo verified that PTX and TBA treatment significantly ameliorated PBDE-47-elicited learning and memory deficits. Collectively, these findings define the HDAC6/microtubule acetylation axis as a core upstream pathway responsible for PBDE-47-triggered autophagic transport failure and neurotoxicity, providing robust experimental evidence and a promising therapeutic target for the prevention of PBDEs-mediated neurological disorders.

title: Zinc activates autophagy by regulating HDAC6 expression following cerebral ischemia/reperfusion injury.
abstract: Intracellular zinc accumulation and excessive autophagy have been reported to contribute to neuronal death following cerebral ischemia/reperfusion (I/R). Histone deacetylase 6 (HDAC6), which contains a zinc-dependent active site, is closely associated with autophagy. However, the relationship between zinc, HDAC6 and autophagy following cerebral I/R remains unclear. In this study, we aim to investigate whether ischemia-induced zinc accumulation activates autophagy through HDAC6. Rats were treated with zinc chelator, autophagy activator/inhibitor or HDAC6 inhibitor during a 90-minute middle cerebral artery occlusion. Infarct volume, neurological deficits, protein expression, and the colocalization of HDAC6, Beclin1, and zinc in neurons were evaluated. Our results demonstrate that beclin1 expression was significantly increased after cerebral I/R and this elevation was markedly attenuated by zinc chelation. Notably, reactivation of autophagy with rapamycin significantly, though not completely, diminished TPEN-mediated neuroprotection, suggesting that zinc-induced autophagy is an important contributor to neuronal injury following cerebral I/R. Moreover, immunofluorescence revealed that HDAC6 was colocalized with Beclin1 in the penumbra of ischemic rats, and inhibition of HDAC6 reduced Beclin1 expression and alleviated brain injury. Molecular docking analysis suggested a potential interaction between HDAC6 and α-tubulin, which may influence autophagy by regulating microtubule stability and autophagosome transport. Furthermore, chelating zinc decreased HDAC6 expression, while HDAC6 inhibition did not influence zinc levels, demonstrating that zinc acts upstream of HDAC6. In conclusion, our findings identify a novel zinc-HDAC6-autophagy signaling axis underlying neuronal injury following cerebral I/R, suggesting that targeting zinc homeostasis or HDAC6 may represent a promising therapeutic strategy.

title: Characterization of human induced pluripotent stem cell (hiPSC)- derived Kidney Organoids as a Platform to Assess Drug-Induced Nephrotoxicity.
abstract: Drug inducted nephrotoxicity is a major cause of withdrawal of Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approved drugs. Animal models and 2D cell culture approaches do not faithfully replicate the structure and drug response associated with human renal tissues. Therefore, the goal of this study is to develop 3D organoid-based models of the kidney to provide a physiologically relevant platform to screen drugs for potential nephrotoxicity. In this study, kidney organoids were created using a process that involves mesodermal induction, organoid , and kidney differentiation. Immunofluorescence imaging was used to profile and quantitatively assess the presence of cells associated with the kidney including endothelial cells and renal tubular cells. Multicellular kidney organoids were then exposed to increasing concentrations (25-800 µM) of four nephrotoxic agents of varying levels of toxicity: cisplatin, gentamicin, dexamethasone, and probenecid. Cisplatin and gentamicin represent high toxicity drugs whereas, dexamethasone and probenecid represent low toxicity drugs. Cellular injury was assessed via evaluation of cell death. Our results show that drug-treated organoids exhibit dose-dependent increases in cell death with significant cell death associated with high toxicity drugs. These findings provide preliminary support for kidney organoids as valuable platforms to study nephrotoxic injury. Further optimization of both organoid maturation and toxicity assays can potentially enhance the reliability and physiological relevance of kidney organoid-based in-vitro platforms for nephrotoxicity testing.

title: SATB2 as a novel messenger of the cGAS-STING signaling pathway drives CUMS-induced depression via gut-brain axis.
abstract: The microbiota-gut-brain axis is involved in the pathogenesis of depression; however, whether the cGAS-STING signaling pathway contributes to onset and progression of depression via gut microbiota dysbiosis remains unknown. This study aims to investigate the role of the cGAS-STING signaling pathway in chronic unpredictable mild stress (CUMS)-induced depressive-like behaviors. Additionally, it aimed to identify novel downstream signaling factors of this pathway. A comprehensive mechanistic investigation was conducted using CUMS rats, HT22 cells, and cGAS+/- mice, with behavioral tests to assess depressive-like behaviors. Changes in the gut-brain axis and the underlying molecular mechanisms were systematically evaluated by histopathological staining, transmission electron microscopy, immunohistochemistry, immunofluorescence, Western blotting, co-immunoprecipitation (Co-IP), transcriptomics, metabolomics, and 16S rRNA sequencing. The results showed that in rats, CUMS induced hippocampal and intestinal damage, inflammation, cGAS-STING activation, and SATB2 upregulation, accompanied by intestinal tight junction impairment. Co-IP assays suggested an interaction between SATB2 and STING/IRF3. Additionally, CUMS rats exhibited altered gut microbiota (decreased beneficial genera, increased opportunistic pathogens) and elevated tobramycin, acarbose, and inosine levels. SATB2 was identified as a potential novel downstream molecule of the cGAS-STING axis, potentially associated with depressive-like behaviors via CUMS-induced gut-brain axis dysregulation. This finding provides a basis for antidepressant intervention strategies targeting this pathway.

title: Butyrate enhances the obesity reduction effect of Semaglutide.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Obesity represents a global public health burden with continuously increasing prevalence over recent decades. Combination regimens pairing semaglutide (Sema) with additional therapeutic agents have emerged as a major focus for anti-obesity research. METHODS: In diet-induced obese (DIO) mice, we evaluated whether oxytocin (Oxt, 3 and 5 mg·kg-1), long-acting oxytocin (la‑Oxt), caffeine, or butyrate could potentiate the anti-obesity efficacy of Sema. We further compared hypothalamic neuronal activity and plasma metabolomic profiles following Sema treatment against dietary restriction (DR), an established intervention for weight loss and metabolic improvement. RESULTS: Whereas Oxt, la‑Oxt, and caffeine did not augment Sema-mediated body weight reduction, butyrate produced significant potentiation of Sema's anti-obesity effects. Either Sema monotherapy or Sema-butyrate co-administration elevated the number of c-Fos-positive cells in the paraventricular nucleus (PVN) of the hypothalamus. By contrast, DR decreased PVN c-Fos-positive cell number. Butyrate amplified Sema-elicited activation of PVN neuronal activity. Plasma metabolomics revealed limited overlap between the pharmacological interventions and DR, demonstrating orthogonal metabolic responses. CONCLUSIONS: These findings identify the Sema-butyrate combination as a promising anti-obesity strategy, and demonstrate that Sema and DR exert divergent effects on both hypothalamic neuronal activity and plasma metabolite levels.

title: CochleaNet: deep learning-based image analysis for cochlear connectomics and gene therapy.
abstract: With the emergence of gene and optogenetic therapies targeting deafness, the comprehensive analysis of the molecular anatomy and physiology of the cochlea has become ever more important. Here, we introduce CochleaNet, a deep learning-based framework to analyze volumetric imaging data obtained by light-sheet microscopy of decalcified, cleared and fluorescently labeled cochleae. CochleaNet covers the workflow from reconstruction of the cochlea to segmentation of inner hair cells, spiral ganglion neurons and their afferent synapses, to the analysis of tonotopy and specific fluorescent expression patterns. We validated CochleaNet by comparison to manual image analysis, also demonstrating its superiority to prior segmentation methods. We then analyzed different spiral ganglion neuron types and validated different gene therapy products with CochleaNet. Trained on high isotropic resolution mouse data, CochleaNet was also applicable to the cochlea of the gerbil, another relevant animal model, and lower-resolution mouse and marmoset data from a commercially available microscope. We conclude that the combination of light-sheet microscopy and image analysis with CochleaNet paves the way for rapid and reliable quantification of cochlear molecular anatomy and preclinical gene therapy outcomes.

title: 53BP1 as a cofactor in the activation of the p53-family transcriptional program: A correlative multimodal microscopy approach.
abstract: Understanding how molecular mechanisms regulate cell function in tissues requires approaches that link phenotypes to mechanisms across different spatial scales. Here, we present automated multimodal multiplexed microscopy for image cytometry (A.M3.I.CO), a correlative imaging platform that combines multiscale resolution, from millimeters to nanometers, with automated workflows for high-throughput phenotypic profiling and targeted single-molecule analysis in situ. Applying A.M3.I.CO, we observed that 53BP1 is recruited at transcribed p53 target genes independently of the activating stimulus, providing evidence for the formation of a putative complex between 53BP1, p53, and the basal transcription machinery in single cells, as also supported by in vivo observations in tumor models. Extending our measurements to p63 and p73, we found that 53BP1 localized at p63- and p73-targeted transcription sites, suggesting a broader role in participating in p53 family-dependent transcription. These findings indicate an additional genome-surveillance pathway in transcriptional control regulating diverse cellular functions while establishing A.M3.I.CO as a platform for spatially resolved functional analysis.

title: Benchmarking segmentation methods for spatial transcriptomics.
abstract: Cell segmentation is a critical yet under-standardized step in spatial transcriptomics, directly affecting cell identity assignment, spatial organization and downstream biological interpretation. Despite rapid advances in spatial transcriptomics technologies, systematic evaluations of segmentation methods across platforms and biological contexts remain limited. Here we benchmark 11 image-based, transcriptomics-based and multimodal segmentation methods across 15 datasets generated by 5 spatial transcriptomics technologies, spanning 12 human and mouse tissue types. We introduce biologically informed evaluation metrics that quantify segmentation quality, transcript recovery, cell composition, morphology, expression purity and spatial organization. Benchmarking reveals substantial variation in performance across datasets, technologies and evaluation criteria, highlighting trade-offs among segmentation completeness, transcriptomic fidelity and biological interpretability. Cross-technology analyses further demonstrate that segmentation choice critically shapes downstream analyses, including cell-type specificity, transcript contamination and ligand-receptor inference. Together, our unified Nextflow pipeline provides a scalable foundation for standardized evaluation of segmentation and method selection in spatial transcriptomics.

title: Chronic thoracic aortitis versus primary medial degeneration in ascending aorta: a digital morphometric analysis of aortic layers remodelling.
abstract: INTRODUCTION: Chronic aortitis (CA) represents a diverse group of inflammatory conditions often diagnosed incidentally in ascending aorta biopsies. While the 2015 and 2016 Consensus Statements on the surgical pathology of the aorta provide standardised histological classifications, data quantifying structural remodelling within individual aortic layers remain limited. Furthermore, distinguishing CA from primary non-inflammatory medial degeneration (MD) can be challenging, particularly when inflammation is sparse or burnt out, and secondary degenerative changes predominate. We aimed to compare morphological changes in CA and MD aneurysms and apply digital image analysis to quantify aortic wall layers. METHODS: Retrospective histological analysis was performed on 63 ascending aortic specimens: CA (n=21), MD (n=21), and autopsy controls (n=21). Digitised elastic-stained sections were analysed using QuPath software to measure the thickness and cross-sectional area of the intima (I), media (M), and adventitia (A). Overall MD scores (i.e., summaries of each MD grade component) were evaluated. Diagnostic performance was assessed using receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis based on binary logistic regression models. RESULTS: CA demonstrated a profound architectural shift, characterised by medial thinning alongside marked intimal and adventitial expansion, resulting in significantly lower M/(I+A) thickness and area ratios compared with MD and controls (p <0.001). CA specimens also exhibited the most severe secondary degenerative changes, with significantly higher overall MD scores (median: 15 vs. 8; p < 0.001). ROC curve analysis revealed diagnostic utility of both the M/(I+A) thickness ratio (AUC = 0.964) and the M/(I+A) area ratio (AUC = 0.955) for identifying CA. A multivariable model combining the overall MD score with the M/(I+A) thickness ratio achieved an AUC of 0.971 (accuracy 88.1%), whereas combining it with the M/(I+A) area ratio yielded an AUC of 0.968 (accuracy 90.5%). CONCLUSION: Digital morphometric analysis provides a reproducible and feasible method for quantifying structural remodelling in chronic aortitis. Changes in the proportions of the aortic layers, specifically intimal and adventitial expansion combined with medial thinning and severe secondary medial degeneration, can facilitate accurate differentiation of aortic wall pathologies, particularly in cases with sparse inflammation.

title: Epidural Spinal Cord Stimulation Promotes the Expansion of Endogenous Neural Stem Cells and Neuroprotection via the PI3K/AKT/ mTOR Pathway after Spinal Cord Injury in Rats.
abstract: Spinal cord injury (SCI) often leads to severe motor and sensory dysfunction, yet no effective treatment currently exists. Epidural spinal cord stimulation (ESCS) is a treatment for chronic neuropathic pain in the trunk and extremities, and exerts a significant effect on the recovery of motor function, although the underlying mechanisms remain unclear. The present study aimed to investigate the effects of ESCS on the endogenous neural stem cells (eNSCs) proliferation and neuroprotection as well as the underlying mechanisms following SCI in rats. In the present study, results showed that ESCS improved hindlimb motor function and markedly increased the numbers of surviving ventral horn neurons of the spinal cord at 7 and 28 days after SCI. ESCS significantly reduced the apoptosis of anterior horn cells in the spinal cord on day 28 post-SCI. Moreover, ESCS remarkably increased the expressions of NSCs markers nestin and sox2, as well as the proportion of nestin/sox2/DAPI-double positive cells (eNSCs) at 7 days after SCI. Notably, ESCS induced only a negligible number of Sox2/NeuN/DAPI double-positive cells at 28 days after SCI. LY294002, a selective inhibitor of phosphoinositide 3-kinase (PI3K) markedly decreased the ratios of eNSCs and surviving ventral horn neurons after ESCS treatment. Finally, ESCS increased the protein levels of phosphorylated-protein kinase B (p-Akt) and phosphorylated-mammalian target of rapamycin (p-mTOR) at 7 days after SCI, and LY294002 significantly attenuated the effects of ESCS on p-Akt and p-mTOR. This report suggests that ESCS treatment after SCI enhances the expansion of eNSCs and neuroprotection via the PI3K/AKT/mTOR signaling pathway.

title: SSH1 knockdown increases autophagosome formation through ATG9A recruitment and promotes tau protein degradation.
abstract: Pathological accumulation of MAPT/tau protein is a defining feature of Alzheimer disease (AD) and related tauopathies, highlighting the need to identify druggable regulators of MAPT/tau clearance. Using Drosophila behavioral assays focused on cytoskeletal remodeling pathways dysregulated in AD, we identified genes whose genetic modulation mitigates MAPT/tau-induced behavioral deficits. These modifiers were validated by histopathology and mechanistically examined in human tauopathy cell models to determine their impact on autophagy-dependent MAPT/tau degradation. Autophagic flux, ATG9A trafficking, and autophagosome biogenesis were further analyzed. Across models, reduction of the phosphatase SSH1 consistently lowered steady-state MAPT/tau levels by enhancing autophagic flux through a mechanism distinct from its canonical regulation of CFL1. Mechanistically, SSH1 functions as a negative regulator of early autophagosome formation: SSH1 depletion promotes ATG9A mobilization to the endoplasmic reticulum-phagophore assembly site (ER-PAS), thereby accelerating autophagic vesicle biogenesis. Importantly, the MAPT/tau-lowering effect of Dmssh attenuation was abolished in flies haploinsufficient for DmAtg9, demonstrating that SSH1-mediated MAPT/tau clearance requires ATG9 function. Consistent with a direct regulatory interaction, in vitro phosphatase assays revealed that recombinant SSH1 decreases ATG9A phosphorylation in the presence of actin, identifying an SSH1-ATG9A regulatory axis controlling autophagosome initiation. These findings position SSH1 as a nodal inhibitor of autophagy initiation whose inhibition enhances MAPT/tau proteolysis. Notably, SSH1 haploinsufficiency also reduces SNCA/α-synuclein accumulation in vivo, indicating broader relevance to neurodegenerative proteopathies. By integrating in vivo functional screening with mechanistic studies in human cells, this work identifies SSH1 as a druggable phosphatase that constrains autophagy at the level of ATG9A-dependent vesicle formation.

title: Tau A152T risk variant drives distinct cell type transcriptional signatures in AD and PSP.
abstract: The A152T point mutation is a rare genetic variant in the tau gene (MAPT) that is linked to risk of Alzheimer's disease (AD) and frontotemporal dementia spectrum disorders, including progressive supranuclear palsy (PSP) and corticobasal degeneration (CBD). To uncover mechanisms through which the A152T variant contributes to risk of tauopathy, we performed single-nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq) on postmortem brain tissue collected from A152T carriers and pathology-matched non-carriers with either AD or PSP, along with age-matched controls. These efforts revealed that despite similar cell type composition across groups, A152T carriers exhibited distinct cell type-specific transcriptional changes in both AD and PSP. Differential expression analysis identified excitatory neurons, oligodendrocytes, and astrocytes as the most affected cell populations in AD and PSP, and these same cell types showed the strongest A152T-specific changes. These findings identify transcriptional alterations that differentiate sporadic AD and sporadic PSP from AD-A152T and PSP-A152T, as well as shared molecular signatures unique to A152T carriers in both PSP and AD. Donor-level pseudo-bulk analyses showed broad directional support with the single-nucleus findings although the proportion of donor-supported genes varied across cell type and comparison. Importantly, merging sporadic and A152T cases into a single disease group was found to mask transcriptional differences in several cell types in both AD and PSP, indicating divergence in transcriptional signature and highlighting the importance of screening for genetic risk variants like A152T in snRNA-seq data from human cohorts.

title: The Spectrum within the Spectrum: Neural Heterogeneity in Autism.
abstract: Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) encompasses diverse behavioral, cognitive, and neural profiles that vary widely across individuals. Because diagnosis remains predominantly behavior-based, clinically meaningful within-spectrum differences are often missed. Recent advances in neuroimaging analysis have created opportunities for the identification of distinct neural profiles within ASD. These new avenues provide ways to examine intra-ASD heterogeneity directly, identifying person-specific brain-behavior patterns that group-level comparisons fail to capture. The present systematic review focused on neuroimaging methods (i.e., resting-state fMRI; rs-fMRI, cortical morphology) that emphasized heterogeneity-informed outcomes based on normative modeling, data-driven subtyping, clustering analysis and similar analytic choices. For rs-fMRI, findings showed that differences in connectivity within the default mode and salience networks were linked to social-communication and language impairments, with subtype-specific patterns emerging across samples. In cortical thickness and surface area, studies identified distinct developmental trajectories and individual deviation profiles, with prefrontal and temporal regions often tied to repetitive behaviors and social-communication difficulties. Voxel-based analyses revealed subgroup-specific gray matter alterations, including cerebellar and cortical differences, that aligned with variation in repetitive behaviors and social difficulties. Collectively, this emerging evidence supports the notion that neural heterogeneity in autism is a core feature rather than a limitation. Embracing individual variability can provide crucial insight into the inconsistencies and contradictions of earlier case-control and group-level findings. Moving forward, autism research must prioritize heterogeneity-based methods to establish reproducible subtypes and individualized brain-behavior links.

title: Conserved SINE and lineage-variable LINE-1 depletion at neurodevelopmental disorder promoters.
abstract: Developmental genes lie in transposon-poor regions, but whether that deficit is a conserved property of the promoters themselves remains unmeasured. Transposable element frequency was compared at neurodevelopmental disorder (NDD) promoters (TSS ±2 kb) in seven primates and two outgroups, contrasting a curated NDD gene set (SFARI and ClinGen; [Formula: see text]) with brain-expressed housekeeping genes ([Formula: see text]). Alu depletion was significant in every primate ([Formula: see text] to [Formula: see text]), including the mouse lemur at 70 Mya. Mouse B1 and B2, SINEs amplified independently of primate Alu, each showed the deficit; the AT-biased Can-SINEs of dog did not. LINE-1 depletion was weak against housekeeping promoters but comparable to or deeper than the SINEs against the genome baseline, and more lineage-variable. The signal survived permutation testing, CpG and GC stratification, and gene-density and recombination controls. It persisted for alignment-defined rather than annotation-defined promoter windows, and against each genome's own baseline in seven of nine, marmoset and dog excepted; the squirrel monkey showed no such exception. Against human controls matched on constraint, brain expression and GC it narrowed but persisted ([Formula: see text]); Alu density does not otherwise track constraint. Windows away from the start site separate two components: the surrounding 250 kb is itself Alu-poor, and a promoter-proximal deficit survives normalisation to it. Depleted promoters coincided with active cis-regulatory elements, preferentially fetal-brain ones. Low promoter SINE content is thus an old feature of NDD-associated loci; whether the elements were never inserted or inserted and later lost is unresolved.

title: Attention Load Modulates Functional Brain Connectivity Reorganization in Children with High Autistic Traits: Evidence from Phase and Amplitude Coupling Metrics.
abstract: Whether emotional processing difficulties in autism spectrum disorder (ASD) stem from deficits in recognizing emotional stimuli or from limitations in flexibly reorganizing brain networks under increasing cognitive demands remains an open question. To our knowledge, this study is among the first to investigate the effects of graded attentional load (low/moderate/high) on EEG-based functional connectivity and brain network organization during task-irrelevant emotional prosody processing in children with high autistic traits (n = 31), by integrating phase-based (iPLV, wPLI) and amplitude-based (AEC) metrics together with graph-theoretic indices within a unified analytic framework. Connectivity matrices from a sliding-window approach were decomposed into edge-level, distributional, and graph-theoretic features and load-dependent changes in connectivity were assessed with statistical analyzes and classification models. The results suggested that attentional load did not uniformly increase or decrease connectivity but rather produced a multi-layered pattern of reorganization that varied as a function of frequency band, connectivity metric, and network topology. Phase-based connectivity in the beta band was decreased with increasing load, while amplitude envelope coupling (AEC) in the theta and alpha bands was increased under high load. This dual-mechanism pattern was most pronounced under the high-load condition, which yielded the greatest number of nominally significant features (uncorrected p<0.05; none survived FDR correction), the largest theta-AEC effect size (Kendall's W up to 0.22), and the best-performing classification model among those tested (accuracy = 72.6%, F1 = 0.725, AUC = 0.764). In conclusion, this exploratory study suggests that, in children with high autistic traits, increasing cognitive demands may be associated with band-specific network reorganization characterized by attenuated phase-based coordination alongside enhanced amplitude-based coupling; these patterns did not survive correction for multiple comparisons, have not been compared with those of typically developed children, and should be treated as hypothesis-generating rather than confirmatory. If replicated, such findings could eventually inform how environmental stimulation and cognitive load are structured in special education settings.

title: Opposing Patterns of the Histone Variant MacroH2A1.1 in Fmr1 Knockout and BTBR T+ Itpr3tf/J Mouse Models of Autism Spectrum Disorder.
abstract: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) exhibits substantial heterogeneity, wherein genetic and idiopathic forms may converge on shared core phenotypes through divergent molecular pathways. The histone variant macroH2A1.1, implicated in chromatin repression and DNA repair, has been linked to behavioral alterations opposite to core ASD features when depleted systemically. However, its regional and cell-type-specific regulation in genetic versus idiopathic ASD models remains unclear. We investigated macroH2A1.1 expression across the dorsal striatum, hippocampus, and medial prefrontal cortex in Fmr1 knockout (Fragile X syndrome model) and BTBR T+ Itpr3tf/J (idiopathic ASD model) mice. Quantitative PCR and imaging analyses revealed opposing patterns: BTBR mice showed region-specific mRNA downregulation and increased strongly stained macroH2A1.1-positive nuclei, whereas Fmr1 knockout mice exhibited reduced strong staining with increased weak staining, specific to neurons and not astrocytes, independent of significant mRNA changes. Bulk RNA-seq meta-analysis and pseudobulk single-cell transcriptomics further identified pathway-level enrichment of oxidative phosphorylation, chromatin remodeling, and transcriptional repression functional gene sets in unmatched public datasets (BTBR striatum; FXS hippocampus and cortex), with pronounced neuron-astrocyte divergence in Fmr1 knockout cortex. These findings underscore distinct epigenetic regulatory mechanisms in genetic and idiopathic ASD models.

title: BHLHE22 monoallelic and biallelic variants cause a neurodevelopmental disorder with agenesis of the corpus callosum, intellectual disability, abnormal muscle tone and movement abnormalities.
abstract: BACKGROUND: BHLHE22 encodes a basic helix-loop-helix transcription factor (bHLH) expressed exclusively in the retina and central nervous system (CNS), and functions as an important regulator of neuronal differentiation. However, BHLHE22 has not yet been associated with a Mendelian neurodevelopmental or neurological disorder. METHODS: Fifteen individuals from thirteen unrelated families carrying BHLHE22 variants identified by exome sequencing were collected through an international collaboration. RESULTS: De novo missense variants located in the highly conserved helix-loop-helix domain of the protein were found in six individuals, and one recurrent homozygous frameshift variant, NP_689627.1:p.Gly74AlafsTer18, was found in nine individuals. Frequent clinical features include absent or limited speech (10/13), delayed or impaired motor abilities (11/13), intellectual disability (9/12), partial or complete agenesis of the corpus callosum (12/15), involuntary movements and/or stereotypies (11/13), and abnormal muscle tone (13/13), depending on data availability. Two individuals developed spastic paraplegia, without intellectual disability (ID) or callosal anomalies. One individual had moderate developmental delay and ID, but without callosal anomalies. CONCLUSION: Collectively, our data establish BHLHE22 as a previously unrecognized neurodevelopmental disease gene. Disruption of BHLHE22, through either dominant or recessive variants, results in a distinct syndrome characterized by abnormalities in brain development, cognition, tone, and movement.

title: Protective role of Galectin-3 in prion disease through regulation of microglial PrPSc uptake.
abstract: Microglia constitute a major innate defense mechanism against prion infection; however, the molecular pathways regulating microglial responses during disease progression remain incompletely understood. Galectin-3 (Gal3), a β-galactoside-binding lectin associated with reactive microglia in multiple neurodegenerative disorders, has been implicated in phagocytosis, inflammatory signaling, and lysosomal homeostasis. Here, we investigated the role of Gal3 in prion disease pathogenesis using prion-infected mice. Gal3 expression was undetectable in healthy brain but became upregulated beginning at late preclinical stages, increasing with disease progression. Gal3 localized predominantly to a subpopulation of reactive IBA1-positive microglia, particularly within the thalamus, and inversely correlated with expression of the homeostatic microglial markers P2Y12 and TMEM119, consistent with acquisition of a reactive phenotype. Microglia engaged in neuronal envelopment displayed elevated Gal3 expression during terminal disease. Constitutive deletion of Gal3 significantly accelerated clinical disease progression without altering total PrPSc accumulation, reactive gliosis, neuronal envelopment, or overall microglial and astrocytic activation. However, Gal3 deficiency markedly reduced microglial uptake of PrPSc, resulting in a lower intracellular-to-extracellular PrPSc ratio, supporting a role for Gal3 in phagocytic sequestration of prions. In contrast, Gal3 deficiency did not impair lysosomal activity, lysosomal membrane integrity, or expression of genes involved in lysosomal repair pathways. Likewise, selective inhibition of autophagy in myeloid cells exerted only minor effects on disease progression. Collectively, these findings identify Gal3 as a sensitive marker of reactive microglia that contributes to microglial uptake of PrPSc and exerts a protective role during prion disease progression.

title: Are 5G radiofrequency electromagnetic fields and PARP1 interfering in the development of human iPSC-derived dopaminergic neurons?
abstract: The rapid expansion of wireless technologies has increased exposure to radiofrequency electromagnetic fields (RF-EMF), with evolving frequencies and network configurations complicating assessment of potential health risks. Although no conclusive evidence links RF-EMF exposure to adverse health outcomes, including neurodevelopmental disorders or neurodegeneration, some studies suggest possible effects on cognitive functions. In this study, we address the role of poly(ADP-ribose) polymerase 1 (PARP1), a protein involved in neuronal development and neurodegeneration, and evaluate potential effects of RF-EMF. Dopaminergic neurons derived from wild-type (WT) and PARP1-knockout (KO) human induced pluripotent stem cells (hiPSCs) were exposed to RF-EMF during differentiation. PARP1 levels in WT cells decreased between differentiation and maturation, supporting its role during early neuronal development. The absence of PARP1 resulted in a prominent increase in dopaminergic phenotype at maturation when compared to differentiation, while protein levels of the dopaminergic progenitor marker decreased. Neuronal maturity was unaffected by genotype, while increased expression of the presynaptic marker synaptophysin suggests enhanced synaptic function in PARP1-KO cells compared to WT cells. Neuronal activity was developing over time in both WT and PARP1-KO cells. However, PARP1 deficiency was associated with selective changes in spike timing and burst-related properties, particularly at early and late differentiation stages. RF-EMF exposure did not alter the neuronal phenotype, development, synaptic integrity, or electrical activity in either genotype. Proteomic analysis further supports that genotype-dependent differences were greater than any RF-EMF-related exposure effects. Future studies should assess RF-EMF exposure at later developmental stages and investigate PARP1 function in disease-relevant models. In conclusion, PARP1 absence was associated with an enhanced dopaminergic phenotype, indicating that PARP1 may influence neuronal differentiation, maturation, and synaptic plasticity. Electrical activity increased with maturation time, consistent with progressive functional development of the neuronal culture. Overall, neuronal development was predominantly influenced by the genotype, whereas RF-EMF exposure produced only transient effects on the dopaminergic phenotype. Evidence of a genotype-dependent response to RF-EMF exposure was observed only for SYP and mTOR.

title: TMEM106B risk converges on C-terminal fragment homeostasis: genetics, mechanisms and therapy.
abstract: TMEM106B is a genetic modifier influencing susceptibility to multiple neurodegenerative disorders, including frontotemporal lobar degeneration with TDP-43 pathology (FTLD-TDP), Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, and limbic-predominant age-related TDP-43 encephalopathy, as well as contributing to healthy brain aging and neuronal reserve. The gene harbours single nucleotide polymorphisms and structural variants that define risk and protective haplotypes, and despite extensive efforts to identify the functional variant within these haplotypes, consensus remains elusive. In this review, we synthesize current knowledge of TMEM106B genetics from human cohorts and mechanistic studies, highlighting how variants may influence its regulatory network and protein levels, with an emphasis on its aggregation-prone C-terminal domain. We further integrate evidence on the roles of TMEM106B within the endo-lysosomal system and beyond, including insights into protein structure, posttranslational modifications, interactors, proteolytic processing, and fibril formation. These findings are contextualized using data from mouse and induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC) models, highlighting current gaps in the available models and the advances required to study its functions and cleavage. Finally, we explore therapeutic strategies targeting TMEM106B, focusing on modulation of expression, specific functional pathways, and fibril formation.

title: Multi-omics analysis of potential therapeutic targets for Alzheimer's disease and associated differences in immune cell infiltration.
abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) represents a progressive neurodegenerative disorder that predominantly impairs the central nervous system. This study integrated single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) and Mendelian randomization (MR) analysis to explore AD therapeutic targets and characterize alterations in immune cell infiltration and function. We analyzed the subtypes, developmental trajectories and intercellular communication of peripheral blood T cells from AD scRNA-seq data. Cell clustering identified CD8+ T cells as the key immune subpopulation in AD, with two vital intercellular communication pathways (MIF-(CD74+CD44) and MIF-(CD74+CXCR4)) identified by trajectory analysis. The expression quantitative trait loci (eQTL) data retrieved from the IEU OpenGWAS database were utilized to perform MR and colocalization analysis to evaluate the association between target genes and AD. Six multiple-SNP and one single-SNP potential target genes were screened via differential expression and MR analysis. Among these, dual-specificity phosphatase 2 (DUSP2) showed a suggestive but weak association with AD, with a mild positive correlation observed in sensitivity analyses. No statistically significant shared genetic signals were detected via colocalization analysis. Additionally, significant differences in intercellular communication were observed between DUSP2+IM and DUSP2-IM cells, with distinct activity across various communication pathways. Gene expression levels in the AD group were significantly higher than in healthy individuals (P = 0.01). In conclusion, this study identified CD8+ T cells as crucial factors in AD pathogenesis, while DUSP2 emerged as a suggestive candidate gene requiring further validation, providing novel mechanistic insights and potential therapeutic targets for AD treatment.

title: Gut microbiota-derived indole-3-acetic acid ameliorates necrotizing enterocolitis-induced adolescent-stage cognitive impairment via regulating AHR-mediated neuroinflammation and synaptic structural integrity.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Necrotizing enterocolitis (NEC) is the most severe acute gastrointestinal disease in preterm infants and is an independent risk factor for adolescent-stage cognitive deficits, especially persistent cognitive impairment. Accumulating evidence indicates that gut-brain axis dysfunction mediates NEC-related brain injury. However, the precise metabolic mechanism linking gut microbiota to sustained cognitive deficits remains unclear. This study aimed to explore the effects of gut microbiota-derived indole-3-acetic acid (IAA) and its downstream AHR signaling on NEC-induced neuroinflammation, synaptic damage and cognitive dysfunction. METHODS: A well-established neonatal mouse NEC model was used in this study. All mice received behavioral tests at postnatal week 4 to evaluate adolescent-stage cognitive. We applied 16S rRNA sequencing and targeted metabolomics to characterize gut microbial dysbiosis and altered tryptophan metabolism in clinical NEC patients and animal models. Hippocampal neuroinflammation was assessed by inflammatory cytokine ELISA and Iba-1 immunofluorescence staining. Single-nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq) was used to analyze microglial phenotypic changes. Synaptic structural integrity was verified by transmission electron microscopy (TEM), Golgi staining and PSD-95immunofluorescence staining. We further conducted microbiota depletion, exogenous IAA supplementation and pharmacological AHR inhibition with CH223191 to confirm the causal role of the IAA-AHR regulatory axis. RESULTS: Neonatal NEC exposure induced persistent cognitive deficits and anxiety-like behaviors in adolescent mice. The mouse hippocampus exhibited a severe pro-inflammatory microenvironment with increased IL-1β, IL-6 and TNF-α and decreased anti-inflammatory IL-22. snRNA-seq identified significant expansion of disease-associated microglia (DA_ Micro), which highly expressed phagocytic genes (Trem2, Cd68) and promoted excessive synaptic pruning. We further confirmed that NEC also induced obvious synaptic damage, including widened synaptic clefts, reduced postsynaptic density, and decreased dendritic spine and PSD-95 levels. Both clinical and animal results showed that disrupted tryptophan metabolism and reduced circulating IAA levels were correlated with systemic inflammation and cognitive performance, respectively. 16S rRNA sequencing confirmed the depletion of IAA-producing bacteria (Lactobacillus johnsonii and Akkermansia muciniphila) in NEC mice. Antibiotic-mediated microbiota depletion further aggravated neuroinflammation, synaptic loss and cognitive dysfunction. In contrast, exogenous IAA treatment relieved neuroinflammation and restored synaptic integrity by activating AHR, whereas AHR inhibition with CH223191 completely reversed these protective effects. CONCLUSIONS: NEC-induced gut dysbiosis reduces microbiota-derived IAA and inhibits protective hippocampal AHR signaling. This metabolic deficiency triggers sustained microglial overactivation, persistent neuroinflammation and synaptic damage, ultimately leading to adolescent-stage cognitive deficits. Restoring the IAA-AHR axis provides a novel microbiota-metabolite-targeted strategy to prevent NEC-related neurodevelopmental complications in preterm infants.

title: Confocal microscopy-based radial profile analysis for submitochondrial protein localization.
abstract: Mitochondria are double-membrane organelles whose functions depend on membrane proteins. Identifying whether proteins localize to the outer mitochondrial membrane (OMM) or inner mitochondrial membrane (IMM) is important but often requires specialized techniques. Here, we developed a confocal laser scanning microscopy (CLSM)-based radial profile analysis for the localization of submitochondrial proteins. Based on this method, cytochrome c oxidase subunit 4 (COX4), adenine nucleotide translocase 2 (ANT2), mitochondrial calcium uniporter (MCU) and calcium-activated potassium channel subunit alpha-1(KCa1.1) signals were spatially distinct from translocase of outer mitochondrial membrane 20 (TOM20) signals in isolated mitochondria. Moreover, osmotic shock increased the apparent spatial separation between OMM- and IMM-associated signals, making it easier to distinguish translocase of inner mitochondrial membrane 23 (TIM23) or pore-forming subunit of the mitochondrial ATP-gated potassium channel (MITOK) signals from TOM20 signals in isolated mitochondria. Our approach provides a practical screening tool for assessing submitochondrial protein localization without specialized instrumentation or expertise.

title: Label-free live cell analysis in transmitted light using cross-channel supervised deep learning.
abstract: Label-free transmitted-light (TL) imaging offers a non-invasive route to monitor live-cell responses in high-content screening, but robust segmentation and viability classification remain difficult because TL images have low intrinsic contrast, poorly defined cellular boundaries, and substantial morphological variability after compound treatment. We developed an AI-enabled workflow in IN Carta Image Analysis Software (Molecular Devices) that uses cross-channel supervision to generate fluorescence-derived ground-truth masks from Hoechst- and Ethidium Homodimer-1-positive populations. These masks are then used to train TL-based segmentation models for label-free inference. The resulting masks were used with TL-derived morphology, intensity, spatial, and texture features to enumerate live cells and support quantitative compound-response analysis. Across U2OS, HeLa, HEK, and HCT116 cells, TL segmentation achieved precision above 0.9 for most compound and concentration conditions, with many conditions exceeding 0.95. F1 scores were above 0.9 for the majority of treatments, with modest reductions in highly perturbed or fragmented samples. Performance was also retained when trained models were applied to additional experimental plates, supporting the consistency of the workflow across experiments. Live-cell detection was the most stable readout, whereas dead-cell classification was more variable in conditions with heterogeneous staining, fragmented cells, or morphological ambiguity. These results demonstrate that fluorescence channels can be used during model development to overcome the TL annotation bottleneck, while the final analysis can be performed from transmitted-light images alone. The workflow provides a scalable framework for label-free cell counting and viability assessment in high-content screening, reducing assay complexity and sample perturbation while maintaining quantitative performance across multiple cell models.

title: Macrophage-derived secretory Clusterin amplifies fibroblast-like synoviocyte activation through PI3K/AKT and NF-κB signaling in rheumatoid arthritis.
abstract: Secretory clusterin (sCLU) has been implicated in inflammatory diseases, yet its role in rheumatoid arthritis (RA) remains poorly defined. Here, we showed that serum sCLU levels were significantly elevated in patients with RA compared with healthy controls (n = 192 RA; n = 139 HC) and were associated with disease activity. Receiver operating characteristic analysis demonstrated moderate diagnostic performance for RA discrimination (AUC = 0.783, 95% CI 0.730-0.837). Mechanistically, M1-polarized macrophages exhibited enhanced sCLU secretion, whereas RA fibroblast-like synoviocytes (RA-FLS) produced minimal sCLU, identifying inflammatory macrophages as an important source of extracellular sCLU. Using a Transwell co-culture system and recombinant sCLU stimulation, we found that sCLU amplified inflammatory cytokine production and promoted the proliferative, migratory, invasive, and apoptosis-resistant phenotypes of RA-FLS under inflammatory conditions. These effects were accompanied with activation of the PI3K/AKT and NF-κB pathways and were significantly attenuated by pharmacological inhibition of either pathway. Proteomic screening, surface plasmon resonance, and co-immunoprecipitation analyses identified fibronectin 1 (FN1) as a direct binding partner of sCLU although its functional contribution requires further investigation. Importantly, genetic deletion of sCLU alleviated disease severity in collagen-induced arthritis mice. Collectively, our findings identify macrophage-derived sCLU as an inflammatory amplifier in RA and suggest that targeting sCLU may represent a potential therapeutic strategy for inflammatory arthritis.

title: The use of three murine genetic models of Alzheimer's disease reveals efficacy of 4',5,7-trihydroxyisoflavone in alleviating cognitive deficits and reducing levels of amyloid-beta and hyperphosphorylated tau protein.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Despite intensive studies on developing therapies for Alzheimer's disease (AD), there is still a need to improve the treatment efficacy. Results of recent studies indicated that genistein (4',5,7-trihydroxyisoflavone) was effective in an autophagy stimulation-dependent improving of cognitive deficits and reducing levels of amyloid-beta and hyperphosphorylated tau protein in brains, when employing a streptozotocin-induced rat model of the sporadic form of AD. Despite those encouraging results, the above-mentioned model has its limitations, mainly related to the rapid and inducible character of the symptoms caused by streptozotocin, induction of other effects (like diabetes) by this toxin, and the requirement for invasive administration of this compound to the brain, in contrast to naturally occurring AD. Thus, in this study, we hypothesized that genistein might be effective in reducing symptoms of AD in well-defined genetic models of this disease and tested the efficacy of this compound. RESULTS: Three genetic models of AD were employed, including mouse lines 5xFAD, THY-Tau22, and 3xTg-AD. Orally administered genistein (at the dose of 150 mg/kg/day) considerably alleviated cognitive deficits (in spatial memory, learning, and long-term memory) of AD animals as estimated using the Morris water maze and the novel object recognition tests. Moreover, significantly reduced levels of amyloid-beta and hyperphosphorylated tau protein in plasma and brains were detected in genistein-treated AD animals relative to those treated with water. CONCLUSIONS: We conclude that genistein revealed significant efficacy in ameliorating symptoms occurring in murine genetic models of AD. Thus, further studies towards the development of a genistein-based treatment for this disease are substantiated. CLINICAL TRIAL NUMBER: Not applicable.

title: NEFL contributes to DJ-1-mediated neuroprotection and autophagic flux regulation in Alzheimer's disease-like injury.
abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder characterized by cognitive decline, amyloid beta accumulation, Tau hyperphosphorylation, and progressive neuronal injury. DJ-1 participates in regulating neuronal oxidative stress, mitochondrial function, and protein homeostasis, yet whether DJ-1 alleviates AD-like neuronal injury by regulating neurofilament light chain (NEFL) and autophagy remains unclear. This study investigated whether NEFL and autophagic homeostasis contribute to the neuroprotective effects of DJ-1 in AD-like neuronal injury. In aged mice, loss of DJ-1 led to learning and memory impairment, neuronal injury in the hippocampal CA3 region, abnormal APP abundance, and increased Tau phosphorylation, accompanied by decreased hippocampal NEFL expression and autophagic dysfunction. In contrast, DJ-1 overexpression improved AD-like pathological injury in APP/PS1 mice and HT-22 cells treated with Aβ25-35, restored NEFL expression, and alleviated autophagic dysfunction. Immunofluorescence showed overlapping spatial distributions of DJ-1 and NEFL in hippocampal neurons and HT-22 cells. Cycloheximide chase analysis further showed that DJ-1 overexpression slowed NEFL protein decay under Aβ25-35-induced injury. Notably, NEFL knockdown significantly weakened the ability of DJ-1 overexpression to improve AD-like pathological abnormalities and impaired autophagic flux. These findings suggest that NEFL contributes to DJ-1-mediated neuroprotection and autophagic flux regulation in AD-like neuronal injury. These results reveal a functional link among DJ-1, NEFL, and autophagic homeostasis and provide new evidence for understanding the mechanisms underlying DJ-1-mediated neuroprotection in AD-like injury.

title: TIA1 is required for microglial activation in tauopathy.
abstract: The RNA-binding protein T cell intracellular antigen-1 (TIA1) regulates cellular stress responses and tau pathology, key contributors to the pathophysiology of tauopathies, including Alzheimer's disease (AD). TIA1 acts in peripheral monocytes to inhibit inflammation, but its function in central microglia, critical to neuroinflammation and disease progression, remains unknown. Here, we crossed TIA1 microglial conditional knockout (cKO) mice (using a Cx3cr1-driven Cre element) with the PS19 P301S MAPT mouse model of tauopathy and demonstrated that TIA1 promotes microglial activation, with a corresponding suppression of microglia activation upon TIA1cKO. We observe striking reductions in cytokine (Tnf-α and Il-1β) and sensome markers (Clec7a, Trem2, and Itgax); importantly, these reductions were accompanied by decreases in tau pathology. Proteomic analyses show TIA1 interaction with the microglial proteins C1Q, previously implicated in microglial activation. These results position TIA1 as a regulator of neuroinflammation and tauopathy in CX3CR1-expressing myeloid cells, including microglia, with potentially divergent functions in central versus peripheral immune compartments.

title: Design and Development of New Dual Target Agents, Cannabinoid Subtype 2 Receptor (CB2R) Agonists, and Fatty Acid Amide Hydrolase (FAAH) Inhibitors against Neurodegeneration.
abstract: As dual modulators of Cannabinoid subtype 2 receptor (CB2R) and fatty acid amide hydrolase (FAAH)an arising therapeutic strategy against diseases based on neuroinflammationwe developed a new series of N-adamantyl-benzamides bearing an anthranilic or salicylic scaffold. Derivatives 18, 22, and 25 emerged as an interesting compromise in terms of CB2R activity, CB2R/CB1R selectivity, and FAAH inhibition. All compounds were potent FAAH inhibitors; 18 and 25 acted as unbiased CB2R agonists with no CB1R affinity, whereas 22 was a CB2R antagonist in the cAMP pathway and partial agonist in β-arrestin-2 recruitment. The three compounds were tested in monocytes and macrophages in resting and activated states and in a human activated microglia model with a potent anti-inflammatory action. These results support the CB2R and FAAH engagement as a promising dual strategy against neuroinflammation providing valuable chemical tools for probing the structural determinants underlying CB2R binding, long residence time, and biased signaling.

title: Development of Organocatalytic Switches of OGG1 that Protect Mitochondria under Oxidative Stress.
abstract: Mitochondrial dysfunction is a major component of neurodegeneration. The mitochondrial genome is prone to oxidative damage, and repair proteins are important to maintain mitochondrial DNA integrity. OGG1 initiates base excision repair of oxidative DNA lesions in both nuclear and mitochondrial genomes. While inhibitors of OGG1 have been extensively explored, pharmacological activation of OGG1 through catalytic reprogramming remains underdeveloped. Herein, we report the discovery of mitochondrial enriched organocatalytic switches of OGG1. Biochemical analysis, mutational profiling, and X-ray crystallography confirmed active-site binding and preferential stimulation of β-elimination over glycosylase turnover, effectively reprogramming OGG1. We demonstrate that ORCAs protect mitochondrial function and morphology under oxidative stress, specifically affecting mitochondrial membrane potential and fragment number while attenuating metabolic stress. Mechanistically, ORCAs improved NAD levels in mouse dissociated cortical neurons and provided neuroprotection in a retina axotomy model. Together, the findings position OGG1-ORCAs as potential novel therapies for the treatment of age-related diseases and neurodegeneration.

title: MiR‑204‑5p modulates glial morphology and apomorphine‑induced rotational asymmetry without dopaminergic neuroprotection in a preclinical mouse model of Parkinson's disease.
abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) is characterized by progressive nigrostriatal dopaminergic degeneration and a dysregulated neuroinflammatory environment. Here, we investigated whether intranigral delivery of a microRNA‑204‑5p mimic (miR‑204-5p) at the time of lesion modulates dopaminergic‑dependent rotational asymmetry, glial morphology, and striatal medium spiny neurons (MSNs) recruitment in a unilateral 6‑OHDA mouse model. Adult C57BL/6 mice received a unilateral striatal 6‑OHDA injection and simultaneous intranigral infusion of a synthetic miR‑204‑5p mimic or vehicle, and apomorphine‑induced rotations, rotarod performance, TH immunohistochemistry, high‑content morphometric analyses of GFAP‑positive astrocytes and IBA1‑positive microglia, and c‑Fos/DARPP‑32 expression were assessed four weeks later. In 6‑OHDA‑lesioned mice, miR‑204-5p treatment significantly reduced apomorphine‑induced contralateral rotations relative to 6‑OHDA alone, while TH‑positive neuron counts in the substantia nigra and TH‑positive fiber density in the striatum remained comparably reduced across all lesioned groups. Intranigral miR‑204-5p delivery in 6‑OHDA‑lesioned animals was associated with increased astrocytic and microglial branching complexity along the nigrostriatal axis and with a higher proportion of striatal DARPP‑32‑positive MSNs expressing c‑Fos during dopaminergic stimulation, without a change in total c‑Fos‑positive cell counts. These findings indicate that miR‑204‑5p mimic administration can modulate glial morphology and apomorphine‑induced rotational asymmetry in a severely denervated nigrostriatal system without detectable dopaminergic neuroprotection as assessed by TH immunostaining. This exploratory study supports further investigation of glial mechanisms in miR-based approaches to PD.

title: TSPO-PET binding in vivo reflects increased phagocytic microglia at post mortem in people with frontotemporal dementia.
abstract: Brain inflammation is a key feature of frontotemporal dementia (FTD). Positron emission tomography (PET) of the 18 kDa translocator protein (TSPO) is widely used as an in vivo proxy for neuroinflammation, but whether the elevated signal reflects microglial, astrocytic or vascular pathology remains controversial, and this has not previously been resolved in FTD using matched ante mortem imaging and post-mortem tissue. We paired ante mortem [11C]PK11195 TSPO-PET with quantitative post-mortem neuropathology in 10 individuals with FTD (5 FTLD-tau, 5 FTLD-TDP) and 5 age- and sex-matched controls, combining CD68 immunohistochemistry across 17 brain regions, multiplex immunofluorescence pairing TSPO with microglial/macrophagic (IBA1, CD68), astrocytic (GFAP) and endothelial (CD31) markers in three frontotemporal cortical regions, and three-dimensional single-cell reconstruction of individual microglia. CD68 area fraction was elevated in FTD relative to controls, predominantly in white matter, and was positively associated with regional TSPO-PET-binding potential across the cohort (β = 8.66, P < 0.001), with comparable slopes in FTLD-tau and FTLD-TDP. Total tissue TSPO-area fraction was likewise increased in FTD and tracked regional PET binding in two independently processed slide sets. Of the four cell-type markers, only the CD68-TSPO co-localised fraction was positively associated with the PET signal (β = +0.0041, P = 0.015, PFDR = 0.062), with null or negative associations for IBA1, GFAP and CD31. At single-cell resolution, IBA1+ microglia that were also CD68+ carried more absolute TSPO and were larger than CD68- microglia, without an increase in the TSPO fraction of cell volume. The elevated TSPO-PET signal in FTD, therefore, likely reflects an increased burden of CD68+ phagocytic microglia rather than TSPO expression in other cell types, supporting TSPO-PET as a microglial-burden biomarker across both FTLD-tau and FTLD-TDP.

title: Progenitor transcriptional alterations link fetal and adult pathology in Huntington's disease.
abstract: Huntington's disease (HD) is an autosomal dominant neurodegenerative disorder caused by a CAG repeat expansion in the HTT gene. Although the mutant huntingtin protein is expressed from conception, clinical symptoms typically emerge in mid-adulthood. Imaging and molecular studies have raised the possibility that HD may involve neurodevelopmental abnormalities, but direct evidence at the single-cell level in the human fetal brain has been lacking. Here we investigated whether early, cell type-specific transcriptional vulnerabilities arise during neurodevelopment, persist into adult pathology, and might be rescued. To address this, we performed single-cell transcriptomic profiling of the lateral ganglionic eminence (LGE) and cortex from a rare, anatomically intact human HD fetal brain, alongside matched controls. These data were complemented by an allelic series of HD mouse embryos and cross-compared with already published human post-mortem brains and brain organoid models' datasets. Neural progenitors displayed the highest number of differentially expressed genes in the human fetal brain, and were also impacted in the HD mouse model, where additional cell types displayed transcriptional alterations. Notably, human HD progenitor transcriptional signatures were moderately enriched in the developing mouse LGE. These progenitors exhibited increased expression of synaptic pathways coupled with reduced expression of cell maintenance genes. Cross-comparison with publicly available post-mortem HD datasets revealed that components of this transcriptional signature persist into adulthood. Furthermore, cellular interactions were found to mitigate these alterations, highlighting a potentially rescuable fetal-to-adult transcriptional signature with important implications for HD pathogenesis and therapeutic strategies. Together, these findings reinforce the view of HD as a disorder with developmental origins, in which early transcriptional changes may shape neuronal function while increasing susceptibility to later neurodegeneration.

title: Breaking the Diffraction Limit: Progress and Prospects of Super-Resolution Fluorescence Microscopy in Biomedical and Materials Research.
abstract: The emergence of super-resolution microscopy (SRM) has had a significant impact on the research field of diffraction-limited optical fluorescence microscopy, which has a span of applications from fundamental biophotonics to advanced materials science. SRM is a powerful technique capable of producing ultra-high-resolution images of organic, semiconductor materials and live cells by overcoming the conventional diffraction limit. In this manuscript, we discuss various strategies for improving the spatial and temporal resolution of SRM techniques without causing photodamage to the sample, which is a common issue when samples are exposed to high-intensity depletion beams. The problem of background noise is also a major limitation of all SRM techniques. In order to address these limitations, we propose various strategies to improve optical design, optical alignments, tuning of wavelengths of excitation and depletion laser beams, fluorescent probes, and microscopy modalities. Moreover, SRM techniques are reviewed and compared with each other as well as with conventional microscopy techniques in terms of imaging properties, spatiotemporal resolution, and fluorescent labels for cancer pathology applications. The continued integration of advanced probe design, adaptive optics, and AI-driven image reconstruction can serve as a future road-map to revolutionize SRM, enabling real-time, non-invasive, and ultra-high-resolution imaging across complex biological and material systems.

title: Persistent neuronal stress signalling underlies Angelman syndrome phenotypes.
abstract: Angelman syndrome is a severe neurodevelopmental disorder caused by the loss of UBE3A, a gene that encodes an E3 ubiquitin ligase1,2. The mechanisms that underlie Angelman syndrome are not well understood, and in particular, the link between UBE3A substrates and disease phenotypes remains uncertain3. Here, using gain- and loss-of-function mutations in UBE3A4,5 along with unbiased proteomics, we show that asparagine synthetase (ASNS) is a target of UBE3A. We find that ASNS protein abundance is increased in the brains of Ube3a-null mice and in human neurons6. Genetic correction of ASNS overabundance rescues microcephaly and many behavioural deficits. Detailed molecular analyses show that ASNS overabundance activates stress signalling and causes a global reduction in neuronal protein synthesis. Our results suggest that loss of UBE3A traps neurons in a state of persistent stress and stunts neuronal growth during developmentally sensitive periods. Moreover, our results indicate that targeting ASNS and the stress response could hold therapeutic potential in Angelman syndrome.

title: The N-Ank protein Ankrd24 shapes neurons and couples to syndapin and the F-actin promoter Cobl-like.
abstract: Proper neuromorphogenesis is pivotal for neuronal network formation and brain function. The underlying cell biological tasks are complex, as they include both remodeling of membrane topologies and of cytoskeletal structures. Yet, mechanisms coordinating these two different cell biological functions are largely unknown. Here, we molecularly and functionally characterize ankyrin repeat domain-containing protein 24 (Ankrd24) and demonstrate that this ankyrin-repeat protein is able to interact with and bend membranes and mechanistically and functionally belongs to the recently proposed N-Ank superfamily. Mutational analyses revealed that the N-Ank functions of Ankrd24 are indispensable for Ankrd24's role in neuromorphogenesis. Ankrd24 furthermore physically cooperated with the F-BAR domain protein syndapin I (PACSIN1) and with Cobl-like (Cobll1), a protein promoting actin filament formation, by ternary complex formation. Both partners were critical for Ankrd24-mediated dendritic arborization. This identified Ankrd24 as critical part of a larger, coordinated effort in inducing new dendritic branches. Our work thereby sheds light on the molecular mechanisms underlying the complex task of proper neuronal arbor development.

title: Cross-species molecular mapping of the photoreceptor sensory cilium and periciliary structures identifies conserved and species-specific architectural features.
abstract: Photoreceptor sensory cilia comprise a microtubule-based structural core and the phototransductive outer segment. The microtubule-based ciliary axoneme extends from the basal body through the connecting cilium into the outer segment, thereby linking the inner and outer segments. Around this central axis, specialized periciliary structures are distributed across the apical inner segment and basal outer segment. Yet how these ciliary and periciliary structures differ between rods and cones and across mammals remains incompletely defined. Using ultrastructure expansion microscopy, we compared their nanoscale molecular organization across canine, non-human primate and human retinas. Key rod-cone differences in ciliary organization were broadly conserved among all three species, whereas the scale and morphology of individual ciliary subcompartments differed between species. Periciliary structures showed even greater species-specific diversification, particularly in rods. Human photoreceptors shared several structural features with non-human primate photoreceptors but also displayed inter-individual variability in accessory inner segment-like structure. These findings refine current understanding of photoreceptor sensory cilia and associated periciliary structures in large mammals, revealing that conserved rod-cone differences co-exist with pronounced species-specific structural and molecular specializations.

title: Suppression of Tau-tubulin kinase 1 mitigates tau phosphorylation, and Aβ mediated neurotoxicity via altered kinase network.
abstract: Tau-tubulin kinase-1 (TTBK1) is a neuron-specific serine/threonine tau kinase that is highly expressed in the entorhinal and hippocampal regions and phosphorylates microtubule-associated protein tau at sites relevant to Alzheimer's disease (AD), thereby contributing to early tau pathology. Targeting TTBK1 can be a promising therapeutic approach for AD, although how suppression of TTBK1 may change neuronal functions is poorly understood. Here we show the proteome and phosphoproteome analysis of murine primary cortical neurons transduced with adeno-associated virus (AAV) expressing short hairpin RNA (shRNA) targeting murine Ttbk1, using tandem mass tag and data independent acquisition liquid chromatography/mass-spectrometry. Suppression of TTBK1 expression by shRNA transduction increases expression of neuronal intermediate filament proteins and V1-domain subunits of the vacuolar H+-ATPase, suggesting the regulatory roles of TTBK1 on cytoskeletal dynamics and lysosomal activity. Silencing of Ttbk1 significantly reduces phosphorylation of TTBK1 and MAP1A as well as increases phosphorylation of neuronal intermediate filament proteins, indicating the regulation of microtubule-related proteins and axonal stabilization. Phosphosite-specific signature analysis identifies the kinases regulated by TTBK1 including AD-related cyclin-dependent kinase 5 (CDK5) and AKT1. Silencing of Ttbk1 significantly reduces CDK5 activator p25/p35 ratio and pT231 phospho-tau level, consistent with the reduced activity of CDK5. Finally, silencing of Ttbk1 reduces amyloid-β-induced neurotoxicity in vitro. These results suggest a close functional relationship or coordinated regulation among TTBK1 and other kinases in maintaining axonal homeostasis via phosphorylation of microtubule-associated proteins, and mediating amyloid-β toxicity, thus emphasize TTBK1 as an emerging therapeutic target of AD.

title: Improved quality and reproducibility of cerebral cortical organoids under microfluidic culture conditions: a proof-of-concept study.
abstract: Cerebral organoids have emerged as advanced three-dimensional in vitro models capable of recapitulating essential aspects of human brain development, thereby offering new opportunities for studying brain physiology and disease. Nonetheless, their use in preclinical settings remains limited by their high variability. Microfluidic devices offer a promising alternative to conventional culture supports by enabling improved recapitulation of the cellular microenvironment; however, most cerebral organoids-on-chips rely on custom-made academic prototypes, limiting their scalability and translatability. Here, we established a brain organoid-on-chip model by combining a regionalized cortical organoid differentiation protocol with a commercial, standardized and industrially-compatible microfluidic device (Duplex™, NETRI). Cortical organoid quality and reproducibility were evaluated using a previously established multi-criteria Quality Control (QC) framework based on a scoring system. To enhance objectivity and throughput, the non-invasive morphometric QC criteria were automated using deep learning-based image analysis. Using a single human induced pluripotent stem cell (hiPSC) line, we assessed whether microfluidic culture conditions could improve the quality and reproducibility of cortical organoids within a controlled genetic background. Compared with conventional cultures, on-chip cortical organoids demonstrated improved inter- and intra-batch reproducibility across multiple scales, including morphology, size, cytoarchitectural organization, and transcript expression, together with higher QC scores and reduced QC failure rates. Finally, the QC framework was adapted for neurotoxicity assessment using a decision tree to classify compounds according to their neurotoxic risk. While this study represents a proof-of-concept within this cellular background, the integrated brain organoid-on-chip platform and standardized QC evaluations provide a flexible and translatable framework for preclinical and industrial studies, and may facilitate future cross-line validation of reproducible cortical organoid cultures.

title: Cas9 nickase-mediated contraction of CAG/CTG repeats is associated with phenotypic improvements in a Huntington's disease mouse model.
abstract: Expanded CAG/CTG repeats cause more than 15 different diseases that all remain without a disease-modifying treatment. Because repeat length accounts for most of the variation in disease severity, contracting CAG/CTG repeats presents an attractive therapeutic avenue. Here, we show that the CRISPR-Cas9 nickase targeted to CAG/CTG repeats leads to efficient repeat contractions in Huntington's disease (HD) patient-derived neurons and astrocytes and in myotonic dystrophy type 1 patient-derived neurons. The approach was allele selective and free of detectable off-target mutations. Injection of the Cas9 nickase into the striatum of the R6/1 mouse model of HD using adeno-associated viral vectors led to repeat contractions in more than half of striatal neurons. Upon injection, we observed a reduction in the number of inclusion bodies, an improved gene expression profile, and amelioration of locomotion deficits in the open field test. The effects were greater than expected from the contractions induced, suggesting that non-cell autonomous mechanisms may be involved. Our results provide the proof of concept that correction of CAG/CTG repeats can improve HD phenotypes in a mouse disease model.
